Directions:
Read the following four texts. Answer the questions below each text by choosing A, B, C or D.
Mark your answers on the ANSWER SHEET. (10 points)

Section II Reading Comprehension

Part A

Text 1

For most of the past century, urban planners treated traffic as a problem to be solved by
building more roads. The assumption seemed reasonable enough: if a road is crowded, add
another lane. Yet cities that followed this logic consistently found themselves with more
traffic rather than less. The phenomenon, now widely known as induced demand, suggests that
the relationship between capacity and congestion is far less direct than the engineers of the
1950s assumed. When a new lane opens, the journey becomes marginally faster, and that
improvement attracts drivers who had previously stayed home, travelled at a different hour, or
used public transport. Within a few years the road is as crowded as before. The conclusion is
uncomfortable for policymakers, because it implies that a great deal of expensive
infrastructure has produced very little lasting benefit. Transport researchers such as
Gilles Duranton have documented the pattern in city after city, and the evidence is now hard
to dispute. What remains disputed is what should be done instead. Some argue for congestion
pricing, which charges drivers for the space they occupy at the busiest hours. Others insist
that the real answer lies in land-use policy: if workplaces and homes were closer together,
the demand for long journeys would simply not arise. Both camps agree on one point, however.
The era in which a city could build its way out of congestion is over.

[A] The engineers were mistaken about the causes of congestion.
[B] Building more roads tends to attract additional traffic.
[C] Public transport is always cheaper than private cars.

21. The author mentions the 1950s engineers in order to ______.

[ C] In consequence [D] As usual
